question: Journalists are our eyes and ears on the ground in Iraq. It is through them that we learn about the country’s struggles in finding a competent, fair, equitable government that, most importantly, maintains peaceful relations with its neighbours and the rest of the world.

Generally speaking, journalists’ stories give a voice to those who would otherwise go unheard and shed a light on things that would otherwise remain shrouded in obscurity. Their field reporting often stops atrocities in their tracks.

Sixteen Italian journalists were due to head to Iraq on 26 April to document the work of Italian troops in ‘Prima Parthica’, a strategic UN-NATO-EU operation aimed at combating international terrorism.

Although entry visas were requested and chased up by the Italian Ministry of Defence itself from the Iraqi Consulate in Rome, none were issued; the Ministry had to call off the journalists’ trip just two days prior to departure. Can the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) say: 1.
What action will the VP/HR take to get to the bottom of what has gone on?
Does the VP/HR intend to point out to the Iraqi authorities that the work of European and allied journalists contributes towards an Iraq that is more modern and at peace among civilised nations?
answer: Following the Honourable Member’s inquiry, the EU Delegation to the Republic of Iraq sought information from the Italian authorities. The latter clarified that the issue was finally solved as the Italian journalists obtained the visas from the Iraqi Embassy in Rome, travelled to Iraq, and were able to perform their work (1).
